source: Kang, Deng, Xiao, Mo, Lee, Bing (2025) First Try Matters: Revisiting the Role of Reflection in Reasoning Models
finding: In eight reasoning models, reflection after a first candidate answer is mostly confirmation. It rarely turns a wrong answer into a right one. The first answer sets the result.
numbers: 8 reasoning models, 5 math sets (AIME24, AIME25, AMC, OlympiadBench, Math500). Over 90% of reflections are confirmatory (right to right or wrong to wrong). Corrective reflections (wrong to right) are mostly under 2%. Reflection after the first answer uses 16.8% to 47.8% of tokens and adds only 1.4% to 3.5% accuracy. Models reflect more on easy sets than hard ones. SFT with more reflection steps (cut-at-6 vs cut-at-1) gains 4.05%, but 3.75% of it is better first answers and only 0.3% is better reflection. Truncating reflection after a candidate answer saves 24.5% of tokens for a 2.9% accuracy drop.
limits: Math only. Reflection is defined as text after the first candidate answer, not as a deliberate change of frame. Does not test an explicit reframe step.
agent_relevance: A generic 'think again' step after an answer is a poor reframe trigger. If O8 is to help, it must fire before commitment or on an outside signal, and it must force a different frame, not a re-check. Supports G1.

source: Liao, Chen, Rajaee, Xu et al. (2025) Lost at the Beginning of Reasoning
finding: The first reasoning step in a long chain of thought has a large effect on the final answer. A wrong first step lowers final accuracy a lot, and models seldom recover. This is first-step lock-in in reasoning models.
numbers: 5 open and closed long-CoT model families, 5 math, science and code benchmarks. Average final accuracy falls about 40% when the first step is wrong (43% on hard questions). Perturbation test (Table 1), accuracy with correct vs incorrect first step: DS-R1-Qwen-1.5B 95.4 vs 64.4; 7B 94.8 vs 28.5; 32B 100.0 vs 85.8; Qwen3-1.7B 96.0 vs 46.6; Qwen3-8B 71.4 vs 37.0; Qwen3-30B-A3B 100.0 vs 74.7; Qwen3-235B-A22B 100.0 vs 78.7. Sampling several first steps, scoring them with a reward model and dropping weak ones cuts inference cost up to 70% with no accuracy loss (Qwen3-8B +1.1%).
limits: First step is a calculation step, not a problem frame. The perturbation is a minor change to the final prediction of step one. The pruning method needs a reward model.
agent_relevance: Direct support for generating several frames at the start and pruning cheaply (a branch-and-prune O8). Also shows models do not undo a bad early frame by themselves.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: GPT-4, GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 are pulled toward numeric hints placed in the prompt. Simple fixes do not remove it. Showing both a high and a low anchor helps somewhat.
numbers: 62 forecast questions, 3 hints each, 30 runs per cell at temperature 0.8, three models. Of 162 paired differences, only 11 had a sign opposite to the anchor. Expert-opinion anchors worked on all 12 expert questions with very small p-values. Chain of thought, thoughts-of-principles (step-back style), 'ignore the hint' and reflection did not reduce the bias on expert-anchor questions (GPT-4 and GPT-4o). Giving both anchors brought GPT-4 near the unbiased value on 8 of the questions where the anchors straddled it.
limits: Anchors came from outside (a hint in the prompt), not from the model's own earlier frame. Submitted to IEEE, not peer reviewed in the text read; models are 2024 non-reasoning. Only t tests, no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Hiding or counter-balancing outside anchors is cheap; telling the model to ignore them is not enough. A step-back style principles step did not fix it. For our agent: show competing frames together, do not tell it to ignore one.

source: Huang, Bie, Na, Ruan, Lei, Yue, He (2025/2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data (SynAnchors)
finding: Anchoring shows up in many LLMs. Reasoning models show it less, but it does not vanish. Common fixes failed.
numbers: SynAnchors dataset (questions built with DeepSeek-R1). Share of questions that are anchored ranges 22% to 61% across models. Examples (total ratio): Qwen2.5-0.5B 60.5%, Mistral-7B 51.1%, GPT-4o-mini 37.0%, GPT-4o 27.3%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%, Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%. Mitigation on Llama-3.1-8B (baseline 34.7%): question-aware prompt 36.8%, knowledge enhancement 50.5%, self-improving 38.4%, adversarial fine-tuning 33.3%, DoLa decoding 37.5% to 38.5%, Anti-DP 24.7% (the one that helped). On Qwen2.5-7B (baseline 40.0%) self-improving was worse at 48.0%.
limits: Version 2 is dated March 2026 and is a workshop paper. Anchors again given in the prompt. Numbers read from a text-extracted table.
agent_relevance: Reasoning mode lowers outside-anchor pull but does not remove it. Self-review prompts are not a fix and can worsen it (supports G1 and the 'hide the first frame' test).

source: Mehta and Datta (2026) When Agents Commit Too Soon: Diagnosing Premature Commitment in LLM Agents
finding: Tool-using agents settle into stable behaviour early. Stability in hidden states tracks low variability across runs but not correctness. A prompt that tells the agent to commit changed variability but not accuracy.
numbers: Llama-3.1-70B ReAct on HotpotQA: step-4 hidden-state similarity vs whole-run variability r = -0.35; replicated on two other models and StrategyQA. The HotpotQA result disappears on hard questions. Of 94 eligible questions, 62 were high accuracy (0.8 or more) and 21 were low accuracy but answer-consistent (confidently wrong). A monitor built from three partial runs predicts variability (mean AUROC 0.81). The commitment prompt cut variability 28% vs a token-matched filler (d = 0.33, p = .001) but not significantly vs the standard agent after correction; accuracy 0.923 control, 0.902 filler, 0.908 commitment.
limits: Measures stability, not whether commitment was premature. Small question set. The prompt changes wording, voice and strategy together. Workshop paper.
agent_relevance: Agreement across runs is not a signal that the frame is right: 21 of 94 questions were stable and wrong. A reframe trigger based only on consistency would miss them. Use token-matched filler controls in our own tests.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Top LLMs do much worse when the task is spread over turns than when all facts come at once. They guess early and then lean on their own early answer. Restating all the facts at the end or every turn recovers part of the loss.
numbers: 200,000+ simulated conversations, six generation tasks, about 15 models. Average drop from fully specified to sharded multi-turn: 39%. Most of it is unreliability, not lower aptitude. RECAP and SNOWBALL (repeat the facts) on GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini, four tasks: SNOWBALL closes about 15% to 20% of the gap; RECAP does better but needs knowing the last turn. Lowering temperature does not remove the unreliability.
limits: Simulated users, generation tasks (code, SQL, maths, actions, data-to-text, summary), not puzzles. Models up to GPT-4.1 and Claude 3.7.
agent_relevance: Larger-scale evidence that restarting from a compact restatement of known facts helps after a wrong early commitment (partial support for the Li 2025 restart trick), and that the gain is partial, not full.

source: Wang, Liu, Liang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place: On the Underthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models that switch between lines of thought too often get worse answers. A penalty on thought-switching words raised accuracy without retraining. Too many reframes can hurt.
numbers: QwQ-32B-Preview, DeepSeek-R1 and distills on MATH500, GPQA Diamond and AIME2024 (AIME 2022 and 2023 for tuning). Incorrect answers use on average 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches than correct ones. Over 70% of incorrect answers contain at least one correct thought. With the switching penalty (TIP), AIME2024 pass@1: QwQ-32B 38.3 to 44.1; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 61.4 to 64.1; DeepSeek-R1 73.8 to 74.8. A prompt-only version for R1 gave 72.4 (no gain).
limits: Thought boundaries are found by marker words such as 'alternatively'. Gains are small for the strongest model. Needs decoding access.
agent_relevance: False-trigger cost: an agent that jumps to a new approach too soon wastes tokens and drops promising lines. G1 should require sustained failure on a line before O8 fires.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen, Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: The bottleneck in self-correction is finding the mistake, not fixing it. With the true error location, correction works. With a random location it hurts.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake, 2,186 chain-of-thought traces, five tasks. GPT-4 overall mistake-location accuracy: 39.80 (whole-trace prompt), 52.87 (direct step), 43.40 (CoT step). Backtracking table (Table 6): with the true error location, accuracy changes by roughly +5 to +44 points across tasks; with a random location, by about 0 to -16 points (column labels partly lost in text extraction). A small classifier trained on out-of-domain data beat prompting a larger model at locating mistakes.
limits: Table 6 column-to-model mapping not fully clear from the extracted text. 2023-24 models, no reasoning models.
agent_relevance: A reframe trigger needs a localised failure signal (a failed test, a contradiction at a step), not a global 'is this right?' check. Supports tying O8 to checkable evidence.

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: Survey of self-correction work. Gains appear mainly where reliable outside feedback exists or checking is easy. Many positive claims come from weak setups.
numbers: Abstract and introduction read in full. The survey says no prior work shows successful self-correction using feedback from prompted LLMs alone, apart from tasks that suit it well, and that the bottleneck is the feedback. It provides a checklist for fair self-correction experiments.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read for this entry; no table of numbers from the body was verified. Cutoff is early 2024.
agent_relevance: Supports firing O8 from external or verifiable feedback, and any test of O8 must avoid the oracle-feedback loophole the survey names.

source: Nori, Usuyama, Horvitz (2024) From Medprompt to o1: Exploration of Run-Time Strategies for Medical Challenge Problems and Beyond
finding: On a reasoning model (o1-preview), classic prompt tricks give little. Few-shot examples hurt, a better task description adds a little, and voting across runs gives the steady gain.
numbers: MedQA (1,273 questions) and other medical sets; three independent samples with error bars. Five-shot prompting reduced o1-preview accuracy on MedQA. Across benchmarks, few-shot was neutral or negative on average, a tailored task prompt gave a marginal gain, and ensembling gave a consistent gain on every benchmark. Cost for 1,273 questions rises about ten times per step ($5 to $50 to $500) across model and strategy options.
limits: Medical multiple choice, o1-preview only, no step-back or rephrase arm.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level reframing on a reasoning model should be compared with plain resampling and voting at equal cost. Expect small effects from wording; plan the test for that.

source: Batorski, Pourhadi, Sarosiek, Spurek, Swoboda (2026) Spurious Prompts: Can Irrelevant Prompts Steer Large Language Models?
finding: Prompts with no link to the task can match zero-shot CoT and task-specific baselines. Step-Back, Analogical and Re-Reading were among the baselines and were not above zero-shot CoT on the newest model tested. A gain from any reframing prompt can be wording noise.
numbers: Seven benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, MedQA, GPQA, OpenBookQA, MuSR, MMLU-Pro), four models from 0.8B to 27B, three runs at zero temperature. Qwen3.5-27B, 7-benchmark average as read from the table: Step-Back 56.71, Re-Reading 58.36, Zero-shot CoT 59.79, PromptWizard 67.99, Spurious prompt 73.24. GSM8K on the same model: Step-Back 54.13 vs zero-shot CoT 83.09. For Qwen3.5-0.8B the averages were Step-Back 38.75, zero-shot CoT 43.84, spurious 42.74.
limits: Rows and columns were matched from garbled PDF table text; verify against the paper before quoting. Zero temperature; whether thinking mode was on is not stated in the text read. The low GSM8K step-back figure may reflect answer-format failures.
agent_relevance: Needed control: a meaning-free or meaning-preserving prompt of the same length. Without it we cannot tell reframing from prompt noise. Also a caution that step-back may not help on current models.

source: Hao, Wan, Zhai (2026) An Investigation of Robustness of LLMs in Mathematical Reasoning: Benchmarking with Mathematically-Equivalent Transformation (PutnamGAP)
finding: Meaning-preserving surface changes (renaming) cost little. Changing the mathematical setting while keeping the proof plan costs much more, for all models including the strongest.
numbers: 1,051 Putnam problems plus 5,255 variants (6,306 items), 18 models. Surface variants stay close to the original. Kernel variant: o3 51.5% to 38.6% (-12.9 points), gemini-2.5-pro 78.4% to 63.5% (-14.9 points). Median kernel drop across models -10.3 points vs -2.1 for the strongest surface family. On 333 length-controlled pairs the mean kernel drop is 5.59 points (17 of 18 models). An expert-solution prefix helps surface failures but little for kernel failures.
limits: Math proofs graded by LLM judges; variants made by an LLM pipeline with judges. Not a test of a reframe prompt.
agent_relevance: Gives a size for the paraphrase control (about 2 points) against a true change of setting (about 10 points). Carrying a plan into a changed setting is the weak spot; an O8 that changes the setting is risky unless the plan is re-derived.

source: Han, Dai, Xia, Zhang et al. (2025) Creativity or Brute Force? Using Brainteasers as a Window into the Problem-Solving Abilities of LLMs
finding: On checkable brainteasers, reasoning models sometimes use brute force even when an insight exists. A hint carrying the insight helps; telling the model not to brute-force helps little. Rewriting a narrative puzzle into a formal maths statement helped two of three models.
numbers: Seven models incl. o3, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini 2.5 Flash. Table 3 Math set, accuracy for plain CoT, Math prompt (discourages brute force), hint: o3 79.6, 79.6, 82.8; DeepSeek-R1 66.8, 70.2, 72.4; Gemini-2.5-flash 66.0, 65.2, 69.2. Logic set o3 68.4, 71.2, 70.0. Rewrite test, 30 hardest rewritable Math items, rewrite by o3 (24 judged equivalent, 6 repaired): o3 56.7% to 73.3% (p = 0.023); DeepSeek-reasoner 50.0% to 63.3% (p = 0.043); R1-Distill-Llama-70B 23.3% to 33.3% (p = 0.08). The paper's conclusion says translation alone 'does not reliably boost' accuracy, which conflicts with these results.
limits: Only 30 items in the rewrite test, rewrite done once offline by o3, no token-matched baseline, grader is o3 (99.3% agreement with humans). Internal inconsistency between result text and conclusion.
agent_relevance: Closest checkable-answer evidence for a reformulation step with current models: a gain on 30 hard items, but not equal-token and not a goal change. A hint (insight handed over) beats a style rule, so O8 should supply a content change, not a reminder.

source: Lee, Kim, Kim, Kim, Rhee, Jung (2026) Are We Measuring Strategy or Phrasing? The Gap Between Surface- and Approach-Level Diversity in LLM Math Reasoning
finding: Common diversity scores mostly measure wording. Candidate sets that use truly different approaches help test-time scaling. Training the model to seek distinct approaches helped more than training on format variants.
numbers: Judge-based approach-level diversity. Moving from 1 to 4 distinct approaches in a candidate set raises best-of-N (PRM) accuracy at M=4 from 63.8 to 65.6 (paired-difference interval excludes zero in all settings for GPT labels). Qwen3-4B SFT, approach-seeking vs format-only data: OlympiadBench avg@3 67.56 vs 55.51, pass@3 69.78 vs 65.78; AIME avg@3 50.00 vs 47.78, pass@3 56.67 vs 58.33. The gain is concentrated on problems where the alternative approaches are reachable by the model.
limits: Math only, small open models for training, LLM judge calibrated against humans; direct optimisation of the judge reward failed (judge hacking).
agent_relevance: Single-ablation signal for gap 10: a different approach (strategy-level reframe) adds value; a rephrase (wording-level) adds little. Test O8 as strategy change vs paraphrase at equal samples.

source: Zhang, Shen, Wu et al. (2024) Self-Contrast: Better Reflection Through Inconsistent Solving Perspectives
finding: Let the model create several different solving perspectives, compare where they disagree, and review from the differences. This beat self-reflection and beat sampling the same prompt many times.
numbers: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2 (7B, 13B, 70B) on GSM8K, SVAMP, CommonMT. Average +7.2% on maths vs -0.51% for plain self-reflection; creative translation +0.95 vs -1.6. GPT-3.5: +7.8% GSM8K, +9.2% SVAMP; Llama-2-70B: +11.6% and +9.3%. Vanilla self-reflection made 20.3% invalid and 4% harmful revisions; Self-Contrast cut harmful ones by 78.9% and invalid ones by 30.8% (GPT-3.5). More than 10% fewer calls than multi-agent debate. Sampling more responses from one prompt stayed below self-made perspectives.
limits: 2023-24 models; Llama-2-7B did not benefit. Uses more calls than single-pass baselines, and the equal-call comparison is only against debate and voting.
agent_relevance: A set of different frames compared against each other gives the review signal that a single self-review lacks. A candidate form of G1: disagreement between frames as the trigger.

source: Gema, Chen, Arditi, Perez et al. (2025) Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute (TMLR)
finding: In some tasks, longer reasoning makes reasoning models worse. One failure is over-reliance on a familiar problem framing.
numbers: Task families: counting with distractors, regression with spurious features, deduction with constraints, and advanced AI risk. Models: Claude Sonnet 3.7, Sonnet 4, Opus 4, o3-mini, o4-mini, o3, Qwen3-32B, QwQ, DeepSeek-R1. Claude models grow more distracted with longer reasoning; o-series resist distractors but over-fit to the problem framing. 'Famous paradoxes' variant: 812 questions (92 without distractors, 180 for each of 1, 3, 5, 7 distractors). Claude Opus 4 and DeepSeek-R1 show inverse scaling; o3 does better as distractors make the paradox harder to recognise.
limits: Tasks built to expose the effect; not typical use. Curves read from figures and text. Reasoning length is controlled by prompt or budget.
agent_relevance: Answer to gap 9: the 'more tokens hurt' pattern is not only clinical. Recognising a familiar frame can trigger a wrong memorised method, so O8 should check whether a frame is borrowed from a known puzzle.

source: Kou, Yang, Hao, Luo, Peng, Han, Guo (2026) Entertain, then Cancel: How Thinking Makes Reasoning Models Read Some and Or Literally
finding: More thinking changes which reading of the text a model picks. Models first entertain the everyday reading and then cancel it in favour of the literal one.
numbers: Same weights, varying thinking budget. GPT-5 high vs minimal effort: pragmatic reading of 'some' changes by -20.6 points (95% CI -31.2 to -11.2) and of 'or' by -18.8 (-27.5 to -10.0). Qwen3-8B on held-out IMPPRES items: -37.7 points for both words. DeepSeek-V4 goes the other way (+8.9 points in V4-Pro, +16.9 in V4-Flash for 'some'). Answering from the early reading recovers the implicature without loss of literal accuracy (exploratory).
limits: Language-interpretation task, not problem solving. Several pre-registered predictions did not hold (the paper says so).
agent_relevance: Reasoning length shifts the frame the model reads into the problem, so a longer budget is not a neutral reframe aid. Log the frame the model adopts at the start and at the end.

source: Dorst and Cross (2001) Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution (read via a hosted copy; fetch-tool summary of the text)
finding: Protocol study of expert designers. Each designer reinterpreted the brief. The creative step was a 'bridge' that fixes a problem and a solution together. Designers who reframed the brief toward newness were among the strongest.
numbers: 9 experienced industrial designers (5 to 20 years), 2.5 hours each, think-aloud; one brief (litter disposal for a Dutch train). 9 concepts rated by 5 design teachers on a 1-10 scale, inter-rater alpha 0.71. Creativity vs total judgement r = 0.32 (reported to rise to 0.8 without one design); ergonomics correlated most with total judgement (r = 0.68). All nine reached the same core idea (separating newspapers). Earlier comparison: 21 students got the same brief.
limits: Text came through a third-party copy and a fetch-tool summary, so figures need a check against the journal PDF (publisher copy closed). Qualitative, n = 9, one brief, no control condition, no causal test of reframing.
agent_relevance: The foundation of the co-evolution idea is a small qualitative study. Treat as a source of the idea, not as evidence that reframing improves results (supports K20).

source: This agent's calculation (2026) Equivalence-bound check for Shin et al. 2025 using their published group sizes
finding: Shin's paper reports no means, standard deviations or effect sizes in its text, only box plots and rank tests, so a real TOST on their data cannot be run from the paper. A planning calculation from group sizes shows what the null can and cannot rule out.
numbers: Assumed group sizes: manual about 62 vs pooled LLM 218 (inferred as 280 minus 218; the paper text gives 280 analysed and 218 LLM users). Normal approximation in SD units: standard error of d = 0.144. Smallest effect detectable at 80% power: d = 0.40; at 95% power: d = 0.52. Power for a medium effect (d = 0.5): 0.94. TOST (alpha 0.05, true difference 0) power: bound +-0.3 SD 0.34; +-0.4 SD 0.74; +-0.5 SD 0.93; 80% power needs a bound of about +-0.43 SD.
limits: Group sizes inferred, ratings are clustered by rater and participant (ignored here), rank tests lose a little power. A calculation, not a result from the data.
agent_relevance: Shin's null excludes medium and larger benefits (about 0.45 SD or more) but not small ones (below about 0.4 SD). It is a 'no medium effect' result, not proof of zero. Raw data are needed for a true equivalence test.

source: Shin et al. (2025) No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing: power-analysis and design details (methods re-read)
finding: Re-read of the methods: the study was sized for medium effects only, and the text reports no equivalence test or effect-size confidence interval.
numbers: G*Power: 220 participants (first analysis) and 280 (second analysis) for a medium effect at 95% power. 456 recruited, 280 analysed. Time per two frames: manual 23.25 min (SD 14.73), direct 21.82 (11.95), structured 28.35 (18.00), free-form 20.78 (9.34). Expert vs novice novelty gap in free-form LLM frames: statistic 2.31, p = 0.06. No test of equivalence is reported.
limits: Whether the roughly 62-person manual arm is the comparison group is inferred. Figure data not machine readable.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays partly open: a design sized for medium effects cannot show a true zero.
